subtopic_detail: bilateral leg pain with a large post void residual and reduced perianal sensation five days after a lifting injury
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 42 year old warehouse worker who developed severe low back pain five days ago while lifting a pallet. Over the past two days the pain has begun shooting down the back of both legs.

Since yesterday morning he has had to wait and strain to start passing urine and feels he never empties. This morning he noticed that the paper felt strange when he wiped himself. He has had no fevers, night sweats or weight loss, has never had cancer, uses no injected drugs and has no indwelling lines. His bowels last opened normally two days ago. A bladder scan in the department shows a post void residual volume of 620 mL.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Reduced sensation over both buttocks and the perineum, reduced voluntary anal squeeze, ankle jerks absent bilaterally, power 4 out of 5 in ankle plantarflexion on both sides, no spinal tenderness to percussion
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60 to 110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Emergency magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbosacral spine today
options.rationale: Bilateral radicular pain with saddle sensory loss, reduced anal tone and urinary retention is a surgical emergency, and magnetic resonance imaging is the only study that shows the disc, the thecal sac and the nerve roots well enough to plan decompression. Outcomes for bladder and sexual function deteriorate with every hour of delay, so the scan is arranged now rather than booked. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Computed tomography of the lumbar spine without intravenous contrast today
options.rationale: Computed tomography shows bone well but resolves the disc, ligament and neural elements poorly, so a normal study cannot exclude compression and an abnormal one rarely gives the surgeon what is needed. It is the fallback only when magnetic resonance imaging is contraindicated or unavailable. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone commenced before any imaging is arranged for him
options.rationale: High dose corticosteroid is given ahead of imaging for malignant spinal cord compression to reduce peritumoural oedema, and the absence of any cancer history, fever, weight loss or raised inflammatory markers argues against that mechanism here. Steroid does not relieve mechanical compression by disc material. (Source: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online)
source_refs: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online

options.text: Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine in two planes including flexion views
options.rationale: Plain films do not image neural tissue at all and change management in acute back pain only when a fracture or gross instability is suspected. Ordering them here consumes time in a condition measured in hours. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.text: Simple analgesia with physiotherapy and general practitioner review in one week
options.rationale: Conservative management is right for mechanical back pain without neurological compromise, but retention with a 620 mL residual and saddle anaesthesia are the specific findings that take this out of that category. Missing them is the commonest cause of permanent bladder dysfunction in this condition. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

explanation.summary: Cauda equina syndrome results from compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus, most often by a large central disc prolapse, and it is one of the few genuine neurosurgical emergencies arising from a common presentation. The features to elicit are bilateral radicular pain or weakness, saddle sensory disturbance, reduced anal tone, and bladder dysfunction that progresses from difficulty initiating micturition and loss of the sense of fullness to painless retention with overflow. Painless retention with overflow incontinence indicates established damage and carries a far worse prognosis than the earlier phase of altered urinary sensation, which is why asking about the quality of bladder sensation matters more than asking only about incontinence. A post void residual measured by bladder scan is a quick objective addition to the examination. Red flags for other serious causes of back pain, namely fever, injected drug use, known malignancy, unexplained weight loss, age over fifty with new pain and prolonged corticosteroid use, are screened for at the same time.
key_points: Bilateral symptoms, saddle anaesthesia, reduced anal tone and urinary change define the syndrome
Magnetic resonance imaging is the only adequate study and is arranged emergently
Painless retention with overflow already indicates established injury
A bladder scan residual is a fast objective bedside measure
Corticosteroid before imaging belongs to malignant cord compression, not disc prolapse
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the patient can feel urine passing and whether they feel the bladder filling, because loss of urethral and filling sensation precedes retention by hours to days and identifies the window in which decompression preserves continence.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

subtopic_detail: fixed airflow obstruction with lower zone predominant emphysema in a woman in her forties with a light smoking history
stem:
You are the respiratory registrar reviewing a 41 year old primary school teacher referred with two years of breathlessness on exertion. She can no longer carry shopping up the stairs to her flat without stopping.

She smoked about five cigarettes a day for five years in her twenties and stopped eleven years ago. She has never worked in dusty or fume exposed environments, keeps no birds and has no mould in her home. She had no childhood asthma and uses no inhaler. Her brother died at forty five of liver failure that the family were told was cirrhosis without a cause being found. Her computed tomography shows emphysematous change concentrated in the lower zones of both lungs with relative sparing of the apices.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, quiet breath sounds with prolonged expiration, no clubbing, no crackles, no wheeze
data_table.Investigations: Forced expiratory volume in one second 48 per cent predicted, ratio to forced vital capacity 0.52, no significant bronchodilator response, diffusing capacity reduced, alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L (less than 35), gamma glutamyl transferase 88 U/L (less than 40)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation to establish the underlying cause?

options.text: Serum total immunoglobulin E with Aspergillus specific antibody testing
options.rationale: This combination investigates allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, which arises in people with asthma or cystic fibrosis and produces central bronchiectasis with mucus plugging rather than basal emphysema. She has no history of asthma and no wheeze. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Serum alpha one antitrypsin concentration with phenotyping if it is reduced
options.rationale: Emphysema before fifty with a trivial smoking history, a lower zone rather than apical distribution, and unexplained liver disease in a first degree relative is the pattern of this inherited protease inhibitor deficiency. Phenotyping is added because the level alone can be misleading during any acute phase response. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Sweat chloride testing followed by an extended cystic fibrosis gene panel
options.rationale: Late presenting cystic fibrosis is a real entity but produces bronchiectasis with chronic productive cough, sinus disease and pancreatic insufficiency rather than isolated basal emphysema with a normal body mass index. Her computed tomography shows destruction rather than airway dilatation. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing with proteinase 3 and myeloperoxidase
options.rationale: Small vessel vasculitis of the lung presents with haemoptysis, nodules or cavities, alveolar haemorrhage and usually renal involvement, none of which is present, and it does not cause fixed airflow obstruction with basal emphysema. The absence of systemic features argues against it. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association

options.text: Cardiopulmonary exercise testing with arterial blood gases taken at peak exercise
options.rationale: Exercise testing quantifies the limitation and distinguishes cardiac from respiratory causes of breathlessness, but the spirometry and imaging have already established that the problem is emphysema. It measures severity rather than identifying an aetiology. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Alpha one antitrypsin deficiency is an inherited disorder of the principal circulating antiprotease, and without it neutrophil elastase released in the lung destroys alveolar tissue unopposed. The severe deficiency phenotype is the commonest clinically significant form, and smoking accelerates decline so steeply that smoking status largely determines whether an affected person presents in their forties or remains well into old age. The radiological signature is panlobular emphysema with a basal predominance, which contrasts with the apical centrilobular pattern of ordinary smoking related disease and is one of the most useful discriminators available. Liver disease arises by a different mechanism, from polymerisation and accumulation of the abnormal protein within hepatocytes, and it can present as neonatal cholestasis, childhood liver disease or adult cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Diagnosis matters for the patient's own management, for smoking cessation emphasis and occupational advice, and because first degree relatives should be offered testing and counselling.
key_points: Suspect it in emphysema before fifty, in never or light smokers, and with a basal distribution
Unexplained liver disease in the patient or a relative is a strong pointer
Measure the level and phenotype, since the level rises as an acute phase reactant
Lung disease comes from unopposed elastase; liver disease from protein accumulation in hepatocytes
Test first degree relatives once a severe deficiency phenotype is confirmed
explanation.pearls: The basal panlobular distribution is the single most useful radiological clue, because ordinary smoking related emphysema is centrilobular and apical, so a lower zone predominant pattern should prompt the test even when the smoking history seems adequate to explain the disease.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: a magnetic gait with urinary urgency and mild forgetfulness in an older man with ventriculomegaly and no parkinsonian signs
stem:
You are the geriatric medicine registrar seeing a 74 year old retired surveyor referred after two falls at home in the past three months. His wife says he has changed over about eight months.

He describes his feet as feeling stuck to the floor when he starts to walk and has most trouble turning in the kitchen and getting going after standing. For the past three months he has had to rush to the toilet and has twice not made it. His wife says he repeats himself and has become slower in conversation, but he manages the household accounts and knows the date and where he is. There is no resting tremor, no rigidity and no reduction in the amplitude of repeated finger tapping. His posture is upright, his arm swing is preserved and there is no postural drop in blood pressure.

data_table.Examination: Broad based shuffling gait with reduced step height and difficulty turning, normal tone and power, Mini Mental State Examination 25 of 30, no tremor or rigidity, no postural hypotension
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography of the brain shows enlarged lateral ventricles with an Evans index of 0.38 and no disproportionate cortical atrophy, vitamin B12, thyroid stimulating hormone, syphilis serology, urea electrolytes and creatinine all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Carotid duplex ultrasound to assess for haemodynamically significant stenosis
options.rationale: Carotid disease causes focal hemispheric events rather than a symmetrical gait disorder with urinary and cognitive change, and he has had no transient ischaemic attack or stroke. The study would not explain a progressive eight month syndrome. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia

options.text: Trial of levodopa titrated over six weeks with formal reassessment of his gait
options.rationale: A levodopa trial is reasonable where parkinsonism is suspected, but bradykinesia, rigidity and rest tremor are all absent and his arm swing is preserved, so the cardinal features are not there to respond. Lower body predominant gait failure without upper limb signs points away from Parkinson disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: High volume lumbar puncture with timed gait testing before and afterwards
options.rationale: Removing thirty to fifty millilitres of cerebrospinal fluid and measuring gait speed and step length before and several hours afterwards is the standard test of whether shunting is likely to help, and the gait component is the feature that responds best. Objective timed measurement is essential because subjective impressions of improvement are unreliable. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

options.text: Referral for insertion of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt on the imaging findings alone
options.rationale: Ventriculomegaly is common in older people and much of it reflects atrophy rather than a treatable disturbance of cerebrospinal fluid dynamics, so operating on the scan alone subjects many patients to a procedure with real infection, haemorrhage and over drainage risks for no benefit. The correct answer is the test that selects who will respond. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

options.text: Electroencephalography to exclude a non convulsive seizure disorder as the cause
options.rationale: Non convulsive status can cause fluctuating confusion but does not produce a steadily progressive gait disorder with urinary urgency over eight months. His clear orientation and preserved handling of the household accounts argue against an ongoing ictal state. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

explanation.summary: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is characterised by ventricular enlargement with a normal opening pressure and the triad of gait disturbance, urinary dysfunction and cognitive slowing, and it matters disproportionately because it is one of the few causes of dementia and gait failure that can be improved by treatment. The gait is the earliest and most responsive element, described as magnetic or apraxic, with a broad base, reduced step height, difficulty initiating and marked trouble turning. Cognitive change is typically subcortical, with slowing, apathy and reduced attention rather than the amnesia of Alzheimer disease, and urinary urgency precedes frank incontinence. Ventriculomegaly alone is not sufficient for the diagnosis because it is common in ageing brains, so response to cerebrospinal fluid removal is used to identify who will benefit from shunting. Reversible mimics including vitamin B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, neurosyphilis, cervical myelopathy and medication effects are excluded first.
key_points: Gait disturbance is the earliest feature and the most likely to improve with treatment
Cognitive impairment is subcortical slowing rather than early amnesia
Ventriculomegaly alone does not make the diagnosis
High volume cerebrospinal fluid removal with objective gait testing predicts shunt response
Exclude vitamin B12 deficiency, thyroid disease and cervical myelopathy first
explanation.pearls: Time a ten metre walk and count steps before and about two to four hours after removing thirty to fifty millilitres of cerebrospinal fluid, because a fall in walking time of more than about ten to twenty per cent is the objective threshold used to select patients for shunting.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

subtopic_detail: confirming the haemodynamic diagnosis before treatment when echocardiography has already estimated a high right ventricular systolic pressure
stem:
You are the cardiology registrar seeing a 36 year old woman with twelve months of breathlessness that has progressed from long walks to the distance between her car and her front door. Three weeks ago she blacked out briefly while carrying washing up a flight of stairs.

She has never smoked, takes no appetite suppressants and uses no stimulant drugs. She has no rash, no Raynaud phenomenon, no joint swelling and no dysphagia. She snores rarely and her partner has seen no pauses in her breathing. Her computed tomography pulmonary angiogram shows no filling defect and clear lung parenchyma, and a ventilation perfusion scan shows no mismatched defects. Her connective tissue serology and human immunodeficiency virus test are negative and her liver ultrasound is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 106/68, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 94 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure raised 6 cm with a prominent v wave, loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge increasing on inspiration, pitting oedema to mid shin
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram shows estimated right ventricular systolic pressure 68 mmHg with a dilated hypokinetic right ventricle, normal left ventricular function and structurally normal valves; spirometry normal with a reduced diffusing capacity; brain natriuretic peptide elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Overnight polysomnography to assess for sleep disordered breathing as a cause
options.rationale: Sleep apnoea can contribute to pulmonary hypertension but rarely produces pressures of this magnitude with right ventricular failure in a young non obese woman, and her partner reports no witnessed apnoea. It is a contributor to look for, not the explanation for this picture. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Repeat transthoracic echocardiography in six months to assess the rate of change
options.rationale: Serial imaging defers action in a woman who has already had exertional syncope, which is a marker of severely limited cardiac output and of high short term mortality. Untreated disease of this type progresses over months, so waiting is itself a decision against treatment. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium to assess the right ventricle
options.rationale: Cardiac magnetic resonance characterises right ventricular volumes and function superbly and is used for prognostication and follow up, but it does not measure pressures directly and so cannot establish the haemodynamic diagnosis. The distinction from the correct answer is measured pressure against inferred structure. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Right heart catheterisation with vasoreactivity testing in a specialist centre
options.rationale: Echocardiography estimates rather than measures pressure and cannot separate pre from post capillary disease, so catheterisation with direct measurement of mean pulmonary artery pressure, wedge pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance is required before any targeted therapy is started. Acute vasoreactivity testing at the same sitting identifies the small group who respond to calcium channel blockade. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Empirical sildenafil started now with reassessment of her exercise capacity later
options.rationale: Pulmonary vasodilators given without a confirmed haemodynamic diagnosis can precipitate pulmonary oedema if the elevation turns out to be post capillary from left heart disease, and they are prescribed in Australia through specialist centres after catheterisation. Treating before measuring risks harming the patient it is meant to help. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Pulmonary hypertension is defined haemodynamically by a mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mmHg measured at right heart catheterisation, and the pre capillary form additionally requires a wedge pressure at or below 15 mmHg with an elevated pulmonary vascular resistance. Echocardiography is the screening test and estimates right ventricular systolic pressure from the tricuspid regurgitant jet, but it systematically over and under estimates in individual patients and cannot distinguish the groups that require entirely different treatment. The classification into five groups drives management: arterial disease, disease due to left heart failure, disease due to lung disease or hypoxia, chronic thromboembolic disease, and multifactorial causes. Chronic thromboembolic disease is specifically excluded with a ventilation perfusion scan rather than a computed tomography angiogram, because the scan is more sensitive for the chronic organised thrombus that is potentially curable by surgical endarterectomy. Exertional syncope, right heart failure and a rapidly falling exercise capacity all mark high risk disease requiring urgent specialist referral.
key_points: Catheterisation defines the diagnosis; echocardiography only screens
A wedge pressure at or below 15 mmHg separates pre from post capillary disease
Ventilation perfusion scanning, not computed tomography, excludes chronic thromboembolic disease
Exertional syncope indicates severely limited cardiac output and high mortality
Targeted pulmonary vasodilators are started only after haemodynamic confirmation
explanation.pearls: A ventilation perfusion scan showing mismatched segmental defects identifies chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, the one form that is potentially curable by pulmonary endarterectomy, which is why it is never omitted even when a computed tomography angiogram is clean.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand
Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: a cord lesion spanning six vertebral segments with negative oligoclonal bands after an episode of painful visual loss
stem:
You are the neurology registrar admitting a 34 year old woman with six days of progressive weakness in both legs, now unable to stand unaided, with a band of altered sensation across her trunk and difficulty passing urine.

Two months ago she had a painful right eye with loss of colour vision over several days, which recovered only partially, and she was told it was probably a viral problem. She has had no rash, no oral or genital ulceration, no dry eyes or mouth and no joint swelling. Magnetic resonance imaging of her spine shows a contiguous cord lesion extending from the fourth to the ninth thoracic vertebral level with swelling and patchy enhancement. Imaging of her brain shows no periventricular or juxtacortical lesions. Cerebrospinal fluid shows 40 white cells per microlitre with a neutrophil component, protein 0.82 g/L and no oligoclonal bands.

data_table.Examination: Power 2 out of 5 in both legs, sensory level at T6, brisk knee and ankle reflexes with extensor plantar responses, right relative afferent pupillary defect, visual acuity 6 out of 24 on the right
data_table.Investigations: Cerebrospinal fluid white cells 40 per microlitre, protein 0.82 g/L (0.15 to 0.45), glucose within normal limits, no oligoclonal bands, spinal magnetic resonance imaging shows a lesion spanning six vertebral segments

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: Visual evoked potentials in both eyes to demonstrate subclinical optic pathway delay
options.rationale: Evoked potentials can document a previous optic neuritis but her clinical history and afferent pupillary defect have already done so, and the test does not distinguish between the conditions under consideration. It would add confirmation of something already known. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Repeat magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with gadolinium in three months
options.rationale: Serial brain imaging is the approach to demonstrating dissemination in time in multiple sclerosis, but a cord lesion spanning six segments, a cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis of this degree with neutrophils, and absent oligoclonal bands are all atypical for that disease. Waiting three months in a relapsing condition that causes stepwise permanent disability is also unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Extractable nuclear antigen antibody panel including anti Ro and anti La antibodies
options.rationale: Connective tissue disease can cause a myelitis and the panel is reasonable to include in a broad screen, but she has none of the sicca, cutaneous, mucosal or articular features that would suggest it. It does not test the leading diagnosis. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association

options.text: Commence interferon beta and arrange neurology follow up within the next month
options.rationale: Beyond being a treatment rather than an investigation, interferon beta is specifically harmful in the condition that this presentation suggests and has been reported to precipitate relapses. Starting a multiple sclerosis therapy before distinguishing the two diseases is the central error to avoid here. (Source: Royal Australasian College of Physicians)
source_refs: Royal Australasian College of Physicians

options.text: Serum aquaporin four immunoglobulin G antibody assayed by a cell based method
options.rationale: A longitudinally extensive cord lesion of three or more vertebral segments with optic neuritis, absent oligoclonal bands and a marked cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis is the pattern of aquaporin four antibody disease, and the cell based assay is substantially more sensitive and specific than older enzyme immunoassays. A positive result changes acute and long term treatment immediately. (Source: Royal Australasian College of Physicians)
source_refs: Royal Australasian College of Physicians

explanation.summary: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder is an antibody mediated astrocytopathy directed at the aquaporin four water channel, and separating it from multiple sclerosis is one of the more consequential diagnostic distinctions in neurology because the treatments diverge and several multiple sclerosis therapies make it worse. The features that point away from multiple sclerosis are a cord lesion extending three or more vertebral segments, severe and often bilateral optic neuritis with poor recovery, area postrema syndrome with intractable hiccups or vomiting, absent oligoclonal bands, and a cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis above fifty cells or containing neutrophils. Attacks are more severe and recover less completely than multiple sclerosis relapses, so disability accumulates through attacks rather than through progression between them, which makes rapid attack treatment and effective relapse prevention the whole of management. Acute attacks are treated with high dose methylprednisolone and plasma exchange for severe or steroid refractory episodes. A separate antibody against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein defines an overlapping but distinct disease with a different prognosis, and is tested when the aquaporin four antibody is negative.
key_points: Three or more contiguous vertebral segments defines a longitudinally extensive cord lesion
Absent oligoclonal bands and a neutrophilic pleocytosis argue against multiple sclerosis
Interferon beta and some other multiple sclerosis therapies worsen this disease
Disability accrues through incomplete recovery from attacks rather than by progression
Test myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody when the aquaporin four antibody is negative
explanation.pearls: Intractable hiccups or vomiting lasting more than forty eight hours, from a lesion in the area postrema of the dorsal medulla, is a recognised presenting syndrome and is frequently investigated as a gastrointestinal problem for weeks before the neurological diagnosis is considered.
